newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan to lower whiskey taxes, raise shochu taxes.
newsitem.headline: Japan to lower whiskey taxes, raise shochu taxes.

text.p: Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) has decided in principle to raise taxes on domestic liquor and lower those for whiskey in order to comply with a World Trade Organisation (WTO) ruling, a Ministry of Finance (MOF) official said on Tuesday.
The revision calls for whiskey taxes, which now stand at 24,558 yen per kilolitre, to be slashed by around 58 percent over a two-year period to 10,225 yen in October 1998.

Taxes on domestic spirits known as "shochu", a potent colourless liquor made mainly from barley, will be raised by about 1.6 times the current rate of 6,228 yen over a two-year period, and will be set at 9,924 yen per kilolitre in October 1998.

Another type of shochu, which has flavour and is made mostly by smaller local breweries, will be raised about 2.4 times from the current rate of 4,084 yen per degree of alcohol per kilolitre over a five-year period, to 9,924 yen in October 2001.
Taxes on liqueur and spirits such as vodka will also be set at 9,924 yen per degree of alcohol per kilolitre in October 1997. Taxes on spirits now stand at 9,927 yen and 8,217 yen for liqueur.
The plan also calls for the government to provide financial assistance to brewers who are expected to be hard hit by the tax hike, he added.

The MOF official said Britain had accepted the plan and the European Union is likely to accept it soon. Canada and the United States have yet to reply formally, but are expected to follow suit, he said.
EU officials were not immediately available for comment.
The WTO, ruling on a complaint by the European Union, the United States and Canada, ruled in November that Japan taxes imported spirits unfairly compared with domestic liquor.

Japan carries out a review of its entire taxation system towards the end of the year and relevant legislation is submitted to parliament early the following year. This would take effect from the start of the fiscal year on April 1.
This year's tax review programme is expected to be outlined on Wednesday.
